one_liner: Ruby 4.0 implementation on GraalVM/Truffle with a partial-evaluation JIT; peak-throughput wins over CRuby and YJIT on CPU-bound pure-Ruby code.
what_it_does: A full alternative Ruby runtime that runs unmodified Ruby scripts, gems and most C extensions; TruffleRuby 40.0.0 targets Ruby 4.0.2 and passes about 98% of ruby/spec. It ships as a Native Standalone (ahead-of-time compiled launcher, starts about as fast as MRI) and a JVM Standalone (slower start, best peak), installed via rbenv/ruby-build/asdf/mise/RVM or ruby/setup-ruby, and can be embedded in Java through the dev.truffleruby:truffleruby Maven artifact. You switch interpreters rather than link a library.
how_it_is_fast: The interpreter is a self-specializing AST interpreter written with the Truffle framework; hot methods are compiled by the Graal compiler through partial evaluation, which inlines aggressively and removes Ruby's dynamism once the program reaches a stable state (the project's own performance guide says it also deletes unneeded computation). Threads run in parallel with no global interpreter lock. Release 40.0.0 also moved POSIX calls and C extensions onto the Java Foreign Function and Memory API (about 100 ns to about 12 ns per native call per the changelog).
when_to_use: Long-running, CPU-bound pure-Ruby code (interpreters, numeric loops, matrix code) where warm-up seconds do not matter: on kostya/benchmarks it ran bench.b in 4.645 s vs 74.107 s for CRuby 4.0.6 and 30.807 s for CRuby with YJIT.
Multi-threaded Ruby that is CPU-bound, since Ruby threads run in parallel (C extensions still take a global extension lock unless marked thread-safe).
Polyglot or JVM deployments that want to call Java, JavaScript, Python or WebAssembly from Ruby in one process (JVM Standalone).
Servers or batch jobs with hundreds of MiB of headroom per process, where peak throughput matters more than RSS.
when_not_to_use: Short scripts, CLIs, or one-shot work that never warms up: on kostya's single-pass Json test it took 10.618 s (JVM) vs 1.031 s for CRuby, and on Base64 3.505 s (JVM) and 8.789 s (Native) vs 1.861 s for CRuby.
Memory-constrained hosts: base RSS about 197 MiB (Native) or 355 MiB (JVM) vs 12 MiB for CRuby on bench.b, and the Json test peaked at 482.80 + 2212.51 MiB on JVM vs 122 + 212 MiB for CRuby.

Code that needs fork, Ractor, callcc or RubyVM internals (not supported), heavy ObjectSpace, set_trace_func or exception/backtrace-heavy control flow (documented as slow), or fiber-heavy schedulers (fibers are OS threads).
Windows or macOS on Intel: supported platforms are Linux x86-64 and Linux/macOS AArch64.

Workloads dominated by YAML, Marshal, regex anchors or certain gems: open performance issues report Psych.load slow (#2089), Marshal.load glacial when cold (#2085), Jekyll slower than MRI after warm-up (#2363) and a primes-utils run at about 159 s vs about 43 s on Ruby 4.0 with YJIT (#4093).

integration.form: language runtime (Native or JVM standalone binary tarball; Maven artifact for embedding in Java)
integration.dependencies: make, gcc and g++ for building C extensions; system libssl and CA certificates for the openssl extension; zlib; a UTF-8 locale
integration.min_toolchain: Standalones bundle their own runtime; embedding TruffleRuby 40.0.0 needs Java 25 (GraalVM/Truffle 25.3.x)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64, Linux AArch64, macOS AArch64 (tested on Oracle Linux 7-9, Ubuntu 18.04-22.04, Fedora 37-38, Debian 10-12)
integration.thread_safety: No GIL: Ruby threads run in parallel; C extensions run under a global extension lock unless they declare themselves thread-safe or Ractor-safe (or --cexts-lock=false); ENV made thread-safe in 40.0.0
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: runs the same Ruby source and most gems including C extensions, but about 98% ruby/spec, no fork/Ractor/callcc/RubyVM, different fiber, GC-stat and error-message behaviour

gotchas: The kostya/benchmarks Dockerfile downloads truffleruby-34.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz and truffleruby-jvm-34.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz, which the project's install guide identifies as the Oracle GraalVM builds (GraalVM Free Terms and Conditions), not the truffleruby-community-* builds that carry the EPL-2.0/GPL-2.0/LGPL-2.1 licence; the guide says Oracle GraalVM is 'significantly faster and more memory-efficient', so the open-source build should be expected to be slower than the measured numbers.

kostya times one run per process between two TCP notify messages, so startup is excluded but JIT warm-up is inside the timed region; this favours CRuby and YJIT on single-pass tests (Json, Base64) and is why TruffleRuby's own guide asks for benchmark-ips style warm-up before measuring.
Performance can drop again when a program leaves the 'stable state' the JIT specialised for; the project recommends running with --engine.TraceCompilation to spot repeated deoptimisation.

The repository has moved: github.com/oracle/truffleruby now resolves to github.com/truffleruby/truffleruby (copyright '2013-2025 Oracle; 2026 TruffleRuby contributors'), and versioning changed from GraalVM numbers (25.0.0) to Ruby-based numbers (34.0 = Ruby 3.4, 40.0 = Ruby 4.0).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over YJIT (CRuby) when peak throughput on long-running CPU-bound Ruby matters more than memory, warm-up and full MRI compatibility (on kostya it beat CRuby --jit on bench.b, Matmul and Primes but lost badly on Json and Base64); pick Spinel or Lightstorm only for AOT-compiled programs that fit their Ruby subsets, since TruffleRuby runs full Ruby and gems.
verified_claims_summary: On kostya/benchmarks (2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G, Docker, same Ruby scripts, Oracle GraalVM builds of TruffleRuby 34.0.1 vs CRuby 4.0.6 built with clang and --enable-yjit) TruffleRuby was about 16x faster than CRuby on bench.b (4.645 s JVM vs 74.107 s), about 12x on Matmul (17.667 s vs 211.868 s) and about 2x on Primes (0.871 s vs 1.794 s), but about 1.9x slower on Base64 and about 10x slower on Json (derived from page data). The peer-reviewed Are We Fast Yet suite (2016 peak performance, normalised to Java 1.8.0_91) put JRuby+Truffle at a 2.36 geomean vs 45.62 for MRI, about 19x (derived from page data).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26, 40.0.0 released with Ruby 4.0.2, 40.1.0 in development) and now community-governed under the truffleruby GitHub org; the Community Edition is open source under EPL-2.0/GPL-2.0/LGPL-2.1, while the faster Oracle GraalVM builds that independent benchmarks use are under Oracle's GraalVM Free Terms and Conditions.
